problem: Sim2real methods handle the perceptual gap and the dynamics gap with separate adaptation modules that must be composed when both coexist, and existing bisimulation representation methods are single-MDP or need true states.
motivation: Simulation and reality share behavioral structure (equivalent actions from equivalent configurations give equivalent long-term outcomes) even when rendering and physics differ. Learning this shared structure from raw observation histories could unify both gaps in one representation and enable zero-shot transfer.
key_idea: Learn a shared GRU history encoder on paired sim/real data with a cross-domain bisimulation-inspired objective (reward prediction, latent dynamics, Wasserstein alignment of successor distributions), then train an RL policy in simulation on the frozen latent and deploy it zero-shot.
insight: Explicit alignment matters beyond co-training: pooled offline RL (IQL) co-training collapses in the egocentric setting (0.17 vs BIFROST 0.50) while BIFROST uses the same data. Ablations show that a W1 dual alignment beats W2 closed-form and MSE-on-means (target return 0.2511 vs 0.2058 vs 0.1263), because MSE leaves the variance free to encode domain identity. Removing the reward or LDP loss also degrades zero-shot return, though only modestly.
method: Paired trajectory collection: sample segments from real trajectories, reset the simulator to the observable configuration (e.g. AprilTag-extracted joint angles/object poses), replay the same action sequence to get time-aligned sim/real observation pairs.
Shared history encoder: a GRU maps observation-action histories from both domains to a latent state z_t.
Reward loss: a predictor R^(z,a) regresses the target-domain reward from both source and target latents.
LDP loss: a conditional-Gaussian latent forward model P^(z,a) is trained to predict the next latent within each domain.
Alignment loss: W1 distance between predicted successor distributions of paired sim and real histories, estimated via a Kantorovich-Rubinstein dual with a gradient-penalty 1-Lipschitz critic.
Policy learning: freeze the encoder and reward predictor, train SAC in simulation on z_t with the learned reward R^, and deploy with the same encoder on the target domain.

setting.backbone: GRU history encoder + SAC policy (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: Paired offline sim/real data: 200 target trajectories (~4,600 paired segments, avg length 32) for navigation; 200 teleoperated trajectories (~6,000 paired segments, avg length 45) for manipulation; plus online RL in simulation.
setting.observation: Nav: 64x64 RGB crop (top-down) or 64x64 RGB-D + body velocity (egocentric) + goal RGB vector; manipulation: 128x128 overhead RGB (+ joint angles for Push-T)
setting.action_space: Continuous: 2D velocity commands (nav), 2D end-effector position via IK (Push-T), joint position commands (visual servoing)
setting.privileged: Paired data collection requires resetting the simulator to the observable configuration extracted from real observations (AprilTags) and target-domain reward; none at inference.

numbers.bench: other:Sim2sim maze navigation (top-down, OpenCV to MuJoCo)
numbers.extra: Uses 200 target-domain trajectories (~4,600 paired segments); 10 seeds

numbers.bench: other:Sim2sim maze navigation (egocentric, SAPIEN to MuJoCo)

numbers.extra: 200 real teleoperated trajectories for paired data; 3 seeds; success reported as fraction

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmarks; custom maze sim2sim tasks and real-robot manipulation. Sim2real is on a real arm, not navigation.
results: BIFROST gets the best result on all tasks: 0.68 top-down (vs BDA 0.67) and 0.50 egocentric (vs Co-Training BC 0.37, BDA 0.34). On real robot it reaches 0.50 Push-T success (vs BDA 0.42) and 7.64° servoing error (vs BDA 8.19°).
limitations: Paired data assume dynamics continuity; contact discontinuities (grasping, insertion) make temporal pairing harmful.
Pairing requires simulator reset from state estimates (AprilTags), so data collection is not end-to-end.
Encoder coverage is limited to the offline paired dataset; policy may exploit unreliable latents on out-of-distribution states.
